- Streaming: not required for initial launch; may add streaming for long-form explainers in Q3.

Thanks Samira — noted on the 512-token tail. We've tentatively booked Thu 4/9 10:00 PT for the bench; Marcus, can you confirm?

Two quick answers up-front so you have context before the bench: 
- Continuous batching: reduces cost significantly at steady QPS by grouping small requests into larger GPU batches. For single-request tail latency, Redwood's serving runtime supports latency SLOs via two levers: (1) max batch size + batch timeout tuning to bound added queuing latency, and (2) a small set of low-latency instance pools (smaller batches or dedicated lanes) to serve spike traffic. In practice you can get the cost benefits of batching while keeping p95 within tight bounds by tuning these knobs.
- Caching: prefix/KV caching is the highest-impact lever for repeat or similar requests (e.g., product description templates). If 20% of requests hit cache, token spend can drop by ~15-30% depending on token overlap.
- Quantization / model variants: we recommend a mixed strategy — quantize non-critical models (8-bit) for bulk traffic and run fp16/float32 variants for the tail or highest quality paths.

Attachments included are the playbook and a CSV with ballpark cost numbers across model variants and batching configs. We'll walk through the CSV during the bench.

If you can share a small sample payload (anonymized), Marcus can run a quick local sim to show p95/p99 tradeoffs ahead of Thursday.

Cheers,
Marissa

Hi Samira — quick technical notes ahead of the bench (see attached brief): 

- Bench assumptions: 128-token avg / 10% 512-token spike; target p95 ≤ 300ms for 128 tokens; p99 target for 512 we should discuss (suggest 800ms).
- Continuous batching behavior: With Redwood's adaptive batching, for steady 200 QPS we see ~25-40% token cost reduction with batch sizes tuned to 8-16 and batch timeouts <= 8ms. During sudden spikes, the runtime can divert a fraction of traffic to a low-latency pool (configurable) which preserves tail latency at ~p95+20-30ms overhead vs pure no-batch lane.
- Streaming vs non-streaming: streaming adds CPU/connection overhead but can reduce perceived time-to-first-token for long outputs. For 512-token responses, streaming reduces time-to-first-token by ~40-60ms in our tests but can slightly increase cost if it prevents certain batching opportunities. We'll measure both in the bench.
- Quant profiles: testing 8-bit quantized variants we observed 1.6--1.9x token throughput improvement on A100 class hardware at ~1.1--1.3x quality delta for prompt completions; recommend a canary on 8-bit for 60% of QPS and keep 40% on fp16 for quality-sensitive requests.

Attachments: redwood_slo_playbook.pdf (playbook) and latency_cost_estimates.csv (CSV). I'll share the bench runbook and the terraform snippets for the low-latency pool in the Drive link prior to Thu.
